title: The kabitts
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas also wrote short Braj verses of great beauty

cards: Some writers have two voices. The same person who writes a long novel also scribbles tiny poems in the margins, and sometimes it's the tiny ones people carry around.
For days now we've been walking through Bhai Gurdas's vars: long ballads, stanza after stanza, telling the story of the Gurus and the sangat. But that wasn't all he wrote.
He had a second voice, in a second language, and it was small. Today: the kabitts.

teach.b: Start with the language. The vars are in Punjabi. The kabitts are in Braj, a language of poetry, written down in the Gurmukhi script Sikhs use for the Guru's word.
Bhai Gurdas could move between them. Then the shape.
A kabitt is a short, tightly measured stanza. Where a var tells a story across many verses, a kabitt has to say what it says inside one. It can't wander.
It packs. One way Bhai Gurdas packs is by stacking pictures.
As this, so that. As a thing in nature behaves, so a Sikh of the Guru behaves. Comparison after comparison, pressed close together, until the last line lands with all their weight behind it.
A kabitt is less like a road and more like a jewel: you turn it over in your hand and the light catches a different face each time. Why does that matter?

teach.h: A STORY, OR A STONE TO CARRY.
teach.b: Because some truths need a story, and some need a stone you can carry. One way to hear it: the vars suit a long evening in the sangat, when there's time for the whole tale.
The kabitts suit a pocket: short enough to learn, dense enough to keep giving. And there's a quiet lesson in the fact that he wrote both.
The same devotion can be told long and told short: a whole life of praise, and a single bright line you can read aloud before the kettle boils.

how: Bhai Gurdas's Kabitt Savaiye are studied and recited by Sikhs alongside his vars, and some are sung in kirtan.

short Persian love songs sung in the gurdwara

p: the script both are written in

s: Bhai Gurdas's kabitts are in Punjabi, like his vars
the kabitts are in Braj, written in the Gurmukhi script.
a kabitt says what it says inside one stanza

games.q: you're a poet with a big truth and room for just one short stanza. what do you do?
o: tell the whole story, very fast.
stack picture on picture until the last line lands.
leave it for a longer poem.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas's kabitts pack: comparison after comparison, as this, so that, until the last line carries all their weight.

practice: If you can, find a single kabitt of Bhai Gurdas in a translation you trust, or one stanza of his vars if that's what's at hand, and read it slowly, out loud or under your breath, twice.
Notice one picture in it and let it sit in your mind; if there's no verse nearby, sit with the last line you remember from these lessons.
